extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, critics, and fans seeking an encyclopedic overview of the novel
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedia article summarizing a single novel: plot, characters, themes, reception, publication history, adaptations, and related commentary. Intended to inform readers about the work rather than provide creative-writing instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalistic depiction of animal behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Adams's descriptions of wild rabbit behaviour were based on The Private Life of the Rabbit (1964) by British naturalist Ronald Lockley.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing on field-accurate sources for animal behaviour grounds a fantasy about talking animals in believable detail; reviewers and scholars note this factual basis as contributing to the book's credibility and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of an internal culture and fictional language (Lapine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rabbits are anthropomorphised, possessing their own culture, language, proverbs, poetry, and mythology; the book includes fragments of a fictional language called 'Lapine'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worldbuilding that includes names, mythic figures (e.g., El-ahrairah), and even language fragments supports immersion; the article notes Lapine is used for naming and mythology across book and adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic/heroic themes and allegorical resonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Evoking epic themes, the novel's labours have been described as mirroring struggles between tyranny and freedom, reason and blind emotion, and the individual and the corporate state; critics compare the story to Homer, Virgil and Campbell's monomyth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of quest/epic structure and classical allusions is a prominent evaluative axis: critics assess how well characters and plot map onto heroic traditions and whether the story sustains allegorical readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and the making of a hero/community
rubrics_metrics.description: The book explores exile, survival, heroism, leadership, political responsibility, and 'the making of a hero and a community'—with central figures like Hazel (leader), Fiver (seer), Bigwig (warrior), Blackberry (cleverness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics evaluate individuals' traits (leadership, bravery, ingenuity, compassion) and how character dynamics produce community cohesion and moral lessons; successful characterization is repeatedly cited in reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative suspense and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers praised Adams's handling of a 'suspenseful narrative' and described the story as 'engaging characters and fast-paced action' that keep readers turning pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tension, pacing, and the ability to sustain reader involvement are key quality markers; reviewers use examples of gripping moments and page-turning suspense to justify praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prose to convey nonhuman perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for the author's 'use of prose to express the strangeness of ordinary human inventions from the rabbits' perspective.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic choices that render human artifacts strange from an animal viewpoint are identified as a strength; prose that consistently sustains this vantage point contributes to thematic impact and originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of gender roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that the does are portrayed as 'little more than passive baby-factories' and that such portrayals fit 'uneasily into the modern world of consideration of both sexes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gender representation is an explicit evaluative criterion: several critics argue the novel's depiction of female rabbits is a weakness or reflects anti-feminist bias; later sequel stories are noted as addressing female prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for children versus mature content
rubrics_metrics.description: Some scholars identify the work as one that 'subtly speaks to a child' because of engaging characters and action, while reviewers warn 'younger children might be troubled by the more graphic scenes' (bloody fights, deaths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments weigh readability and themes appropriate for children against violent or 'grim' material; suitability is judged by narrative tone, graphic content, and didactic/subtle elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldbuilding consistency and imaginative civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers credit Adams's 'consistent, comprehensible and altogether enchanting civilisation' created for the rabbits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coherent, internally consistent culture-building (myth, social structures like Owsla, naming conventions) is cited as a major achievement and criterion for literary success in fantasy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation choices and fidelity (film, TV, stage, audio, graphic novel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adaptations omit side plots and vary in tone and quality; the 1978 film 'omitted several side plots' but 'cut through Adams' book... to get to the beating heart', while the 2018 series received praise for voice acting but criticism for tone and computer animation quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating adaptations, critics consider fidelity (what is omitted or compressed), tone, medium-specific execution (animation quality, voice performances), and whether the adaptation captures the novel's thematic core.
